name: Wycliffe's doctrine of civil dominion and its escalation into heresy
plain_explanation: Wycliffe, orthodox until his fifties, argued in 1376 lectures 'On Civil Dominion' that righteousness alone gives title to dominion and property, that unrighteous clergy therefore have no valid title to theirs, and that civil (not ecclesiastical) authority should decide whether a cleric keeps his property. From there he escalated: property itself is a result of sin (Christ and the Apostles owned none, so clergy should own none either); during the Great Schism he branded the Pope Antichrist and argued the Donation of Constantine had made all subsequent popes apostates; he translated the Vulgate into English and founded itinerant 'poor priests'; and finally he denied transubstantiation outright, calling it 'a deceit and a blasphemous folly.'
precise_definition: Wycliffe's progressively radicalizing theological-political doctrine, beginning from the claim that righteousness (not mere possession) grounds legitimate dominion and property, and ending in outright denial of transubstantiation and denunciation of the papacy as apostate.
why_it_mattered: It exemplifies, for Russell, how a movement driven initially by moral and political conviction (sympathy for the poor, horror of clerical wealth) could be driven by its own logic into full doctrinal heresy, and it directly seeded both the English Lollard movement and, via Huss, the pre-Reformation Bohemian Hussite movement.
historical_origin: Begins with Wycliffe's 1376 Oxford lectures 'On Civil Dominion,' escalating through the Great Schism (from 1378) to his death in 1384.
examples: English royal support for Wycliffe's doctrines, since they justified withholding tribute money from a Pope subservient to France, especially convenient during England's war with France
The University of Oxford's refusal to admit papal jurisdiction over its own teachers, protecting Wycliffe from a bishops' tribunal
The House of Commons's refusal to concur when the House of Lords condemned Wycliffe's itinerant 'poor priests'
objections: Gregory XI condemned eighteen theses in Wycliffe's lectures, charging they derived from Marsiglio of Padua
influence_on_later_thinkers: His English followers, the Lollards, were persecuted and largely suppressed, but his doctrines reached Bohemia (via the marriage of Richard II to a Bohemian princess) where Huss became his disciple and the movement survived, despite persecution, until the Reformation.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Deeply political from the outset: John of Gaunt protected Wycliffe as long as politically convenient, and the doctrine's appeal to the English crown was inseparable from anti-French, anti-papal-tribute politics.
